Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) served as a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). He grew up in Tasmania and became an air cadet in the RAAF in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he focused on flight training and navigation. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, which operated Lockheed Hudson aircraft. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December, where it engaged in combat against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. After returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam took on various staff and training positions, ultimately concluding the war with the rank of group captain.

In 1946, Headlam was the Officer Commanding for the North Western Area, and from 1947 to 1950, he assumed the position of Director of Training. During the Malayan Emergency between 1950 and 1951, he was stationed in Singapore, where he commanded No. 90 (Composite) Wing and later RAF Tengah. He held the role of Air Member for Personnel on two occasions, first in 1957 and then from 1959 to 1960. In 1958, he was honored with the title of Commander of the Order of the British Empire. After being promoted to air vice marshal, he occupied several key roles, including Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961 to 1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff from 1965 to 1966, and AOC Support Command from 1966 to 1967. He was also recognized as a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. Following his tenure leading the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam was born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, to farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He completed his matriculation at <unk> College in Hobart in 1932. Despite his parents' objections, he enlisted as an air cadet in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) on January 16, 1934. Frank received his flying training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook in Victoria and was commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

After completing a conversion course, Headlam was assigned to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. The official history of the pre-war Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) indicates that the Seaplane Squadron had a limited flight size and was part of No. 1 Flying Training School, operating aircraft like the Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, among others. During this time, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense in which he argued that Australia could be made nearly invulnerable with "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens remarked that this paper "effectively defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which has been a consistent element of RAAF strategic thought."

In July 1936, Headlam completed a flying instructor course and subsequently joined No. 1 FTS. He was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Beginning in July 1938, he participated in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, which was conducted by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured several significant training flights that garnered substantial media attention, including a notable twelve-day, 10,800-kilometre (6,700 mi) journey around Australia in November, during which Headlam piloted one of three Avro Ansons. The next month, he commanded the three Ansons on a six-day expedition over Central Australia. He excelled in the navigation course, receiving special acknowledgment for his performance. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander. Initially, he served with No. 2 Squadron before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, with both squadrons utilizing Ansons.

After the onset of World War II, No. 1 Squadron engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance operations along Australia's southeastern coast. Headlam continued to serve as a flight commander in the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to assume the position of station navigation officer. On March 27, he became part of the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was promoted to squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Just two weeks later, he wed Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and they would later have a son and a daughter.

On 15 April 1941, Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron based at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander on 1 July. The squadron, outfitted with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily carried out maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December, when four of its aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns over potential Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On 7 December, this group began operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron remained on standby in Darwin. The next day, after confirming that Australia was now engaged in war in the Pacific, one of the Hudsons at Penfui targeted the Japanese vessel Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship, and successfully forced it aground. By 12 December, Headlam had moved to Penfui, assuming the role of commanding officer for both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, the aircraft of No. 2 Squadron were stationed at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The unit based in Penfui conducted operations targeting Japanese shipping involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudson bombers engaged three Japanese floatplanes that were bombarding a transport vessel, successfully managing to shoot down or damage some of the enemy aircraft. However, the following day, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. The Japanese launched their first bombing raid on Penfui on January 26, 1942, with subsequent attacks causing damage to several aircraft. The Hudsons that remained operational were transferred to Darwin, while Headlam and his crew stayed at Penfui to oversee reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam was instructed to evacuate all personnel except for a small team to assist in demolishing the airfield with the help of Sparrow Force. He returned to Darwin the next day, just as the city experienced its first Japanese air raid. During this assault, four Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron were destroyed, and the remaining planes were moved to Daly Waters, where they continued their reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese troops in Timor.

Headlam held his role as the Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command in Darwin until May 12, 1942, when he was assigned to Nhill, Victoria, to serve as the commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Ansons. In June, the personnel from this school established No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School ( <unk> ), which also utilized Ansons and was situated in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was promoted to group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3 <unk>, which operated Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. Following the transfer of command of No. 3 <unk>, he began his studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. On January 12, 1945, he was appointed as the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam was designated as the Officer Commanding the North Western Area. By the year's conclusion, he was relocated back to Britain, where he enrolled in the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked alongside the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon his return to Australia in November 1947, he took on the role of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, he succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as the leader of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, based at RAF Changi in Singapore. No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units that participated in the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which operated Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, which flew Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns performed area bombing in communist-held territories and targeted specific locations, while the Dakotas managed courier operations, transported VIPs, facilitated medical evacuations throughout Southeast Asia, airlifted troops and supplies, and distributed propaganda leaflets in Malaya. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a Dakota from No. 38 Squadron, which he was co-piloting during a supply drop, crash-landed in Kampong Aur, Pahang, due to engine failure. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah in Singapore while still serving as the commanding officer of No. 90 Wing, which he handed over in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam took on the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command located in Penrith, New South Wales. While serving as SASO, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) began modernizing its fleet with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also experienced a significant organizational change, moving from a geography-based command-and-control system to a functionally organized structure. This shift led to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. In October 1953, Eastern Area Command, which had effectively been operating as an operational headquarters due to the number of combat units it oversaw, was reorganized into Home Command. In recognition of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and on October 7, 1954, it was announced that he would take on the role of aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II.

On 1 January 1955, Headlam was elevated to the rank of substantive air commodore. Later that November, he was posted to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and the following year, he commenced his studies at the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he served as the Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from 19 March to 21 October 1957, filling the interim role between Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this capacity, Headlam participated in the Air Board, the governing body of the service made up of its senior officers and headed by the Chief of the Air Staff. He was also one of two RAAF representatives on a committee led by businessman William John Allison, which assessed defense service conditions; the committee's findings resulted in a significant increase in flight pay, among other advantages. Furthermore, Headlam held additional roles within the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, the latter placing him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. He was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) during the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, which were announced on 3 June. In May 1960, he took on the role of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam became a member of the Operational Command (OPCOM) team, which had taken over the responsibilities from Home Command to oversee RAAF operational units. In April, he succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as the Air Officer Commanding (AOC) of OPCOM. He achieved the rank of air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, he was assigned to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and just a week later, he assumed the role of AOC for No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch took over from him as AOC OPCOM. While serving as AOC for No. 224 Group, Headlam was in charge of regional air defense and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, followed by the onset of the Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which formally began the next month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married the widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He transferred command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam took on the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on 26 January 1965. He received the honor of Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on 22 June in recognition of his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His time as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament initiative the Air Force had embarked upon since World War II, which was further complicated by staffing shortages resulting from this expansion and Australia's growing security obligations in Southeast Asia. Towards the end of his tenure, the first RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War; in March 1966, he visited Saigon alongside Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to discuss deployment strategies. A year prior, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, the idea of sending two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for training, but Murdoch declined the proposal, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron ill-prepared for its cooperative role with the army upon arrival. On 8 August 1966, Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as Air Officer Commanding Support Command in Melbourne, which had been established in 1959 through the merger of the RAAF’s earlier Training and Maintenance Commands. He was subsequently appointed to London on 1 January 1968 as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. Additionally, he served as Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971.

Upon his return to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took a period of resettlement leave prior to his retirement from the Air Force on August 3. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a lengthy struggle with cancer. He is survived by his children and his second spouse. A private funeral service was held, and he was cremated at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a significant trunkline located in the Lower Peninsula of Michigan, USA, connecting Fremont and Howard City. The stretch between Newaygo and Howard City passes through Fremont and runs along the southern border of the Manistee National Forest. This iteration of M-82 is the state's second; the original was created in the Upper Peninsula circa 1919. The Lower Peninsula route has remained largely unchanged since the 1920s, although there have been various extensions and reductions that have adjusted the endpoint to as far west as New Era or Hesperia. The current alignment was established in the late 1970s.

M @-@ 82 starts at an intersection with M @-@ 120 and B @-@ 96, located to the west of Fremont. This intersection marks the convergence of three county lines. M @-@ 120 serves as the north-south boundary between Newaygo and Oceana counties, as well as between Newaygo and Muskegon counties. B @-@ 96 delineates the east-west boundary for Oceana and Muskegon counties, extending directly to the west of the junction. M @-@ 82 travels eastward from this point, following 48th Street through agricultural areas until it arrives in Fremont. Upon entering the town, it becomes Main Street, navigating through the downtown district before M @-@ 82 turns south onto Stewart Avenue when leaving the city. The highway then curves onto 72nd Street, continuing eastward through additional farming landscapes. As M @-@ 82 approaches Newaygo, the environment becomes increasingly forested near the Muskegon River. The route carries on along Fremont Street until it intersects with M @-@ 37. The two highways merge, crossing the river and entering downtown along State Street. Just south of downtown, M @-@ 82 shifts east once more, separating from M @-@ 37, and follows 82nd Street along the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of M @-@ 82 is located at exit 118 on US 131 / M @-@ 46, to the west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) oversees the upkeep of its roadways and consistently tracks the traffic flow on them. This traffic flow is evaluated using a measurement called average annual daily traffic (AADT), which reflects the typical number of vehicles that traverse a particular road segment each day throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT reported that the peak traffic volume on M-82, situated to the west of Fremont, was 16,532 vehicles per day. Conversely, the lowest volume recorded was 4,018 vehicles to the east of Newaygo. Furthermore, MDOT has not designated any portion of this highway as part of the National Highway System, which comprises roads essential to the country's economy, defense, and transportation infrastructure.

The current M-82 was established in 1926, stretching from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. This route passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over the previous M-41 alignment. In late 1936, M-46 was extended to link Newaygo with Howard City, creating a concurrency with M-82 to bridge a gap in the M-46 route. By 1938, this shared section was designated exclusively as M-46, which reverted M-82 to its northern intersection with M-37 in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was rerouted along a new path west of Ferry, changing its trajectory from northwest toward Hart to a westbound endpoint in Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western segment of the highway underwent two realignments, extending from Hesperia to New Era while bypassing Ferry. A significant alteration occurred around 1969, prompting a change in highway designations within Oceana County. M-20 replaced M-82 to the west of Hesperia, terminating at New Era rather than Muskegon. At the same time, M-120 took over the section south of Hesperia, and M-82 was restricted to the route connecting Hesperia and Newaygo. In 1973, the highway's length was extended as the eastern terminus was shifted back to Howard City. M-46 was redirected to link with the US 131 freeway from Howard City to Cedar Springs, assuming control of M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This adjustment allowed the segment from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final modification occurred in 1978, when the overlap with M-120 was removed, favoring M-120 instead. Consequently, the M-82 designation was limited to the junction west of Fremont, solidifying the current route of the highway.

Shikamaru Nara (Nara Shikamaru) is a character from the Naruto manga and anime series, which was created by Masashi Kishimoto. However, beneath his laid-back exterior lies remarkable intelligence; his mentor, Asuma Sarutobi, assessed Shikamaru's IQ to be over 200. Although Shikamaru's team successfully overcomes the Otogakure ninjas they encounter, Sasuke still succeeds in escaping.

Following the fight, Shikamaru promises to look after Kurenai and Asuma's newborn daughter. He is later placed in the Fourth Division alongside Temari and another comrade, acting as a proxy general under Gaara. Shikamaru has consistently performed well in the Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls, frequently landing in the top ten and notably achieving fourth place at least once. The most recent poll, conducted in 2011, saw Shikamaru finishing in ninth place, positioned between Sasori and Hinata. A range of merchandise featuring Shikamaru has been produced, including action figures, keychains, and patches that showcase his appearances from both Part I and Part II. Additionally, customers of NTT have ranked him as the sixteenth most popular black-haired male anime character. Hiroshi Matsuyama, the CEO of CyberConnect2, has expressed that Shikamaru is among his favorite characters from Naruto.

A multitude of articles focusing on manga, anime, video games, and similar media have examined Shikamaru's character. IGN identified Shikamaru as one of their favorite characters in the series, referring to him as "the poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" because of his general apathy and reluctance to fulfill his potential. In their review of episode 110, IGN commended Shikamaru for overcoming his lazy habits and stepping up as a leader during the mission to rescue Sasuke Uchiha, agreeing that his promotion to Chunin was well-earned. Anime News Network also remarked on this transformation, describing Shikamaru's growth into "an unlikely hero" as a standout moment of the arc. In a later review of episode 135, where the mission to save Sasuke failed and Shikamaru's team suffered significant injuries, IGN highlighted the "great moment" when Shikamaru wept upon learning that his friends would recover, stressing that he would develop into a better leader for them. Justin Rich from Mania Entertainment praised Shikamaru's "sheer intellect," calling him "one of the most intriguing characters in the series" and "one of the few truly brilliant fighters in shōnen anime." Dani Moure, another reviewer from the same outlet, pointed out Shikamaru's battle against Temari during the Chunin Exams as "one of the better fights featuring supporting characters."

Meridian is the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA, serving as the county seat for Lauderdale County. It is the main city within the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. This city is conveniently located along key highways, positioned 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 at the crossroads of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian's economy developed around the railroads and the goods they carried, establishing it as a significant trading hub. In February 1864, during the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman set fire to a substantial portion of the city during the Battle of Meridian.

After the war, the city underwent a period of rebuilding and entered a phase known as a "Golden Age," during which it grew to become the largest city in Mississippi from 1890 to 1930 and evolved into a notable manufacturing hub in the South, with 44 trains arriving and departing each day. Union Station, which opened in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal transportation center, linking to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, accommodating around 242,360 passengers annually. Despite facing economic difficulties due to a downturn in the railroad industry, the city successfully diversified its economy, with the healthcare, military, and manufacturing industries providing most of the jobs by 2010. According to the 2008 census, the estimated population within the city limits is 38,232, while the larger population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius is 232,900, and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with 104,600 and 234,200 individuals respectively contributing to the labor force and supporting the city's economy.

The region is served by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively offer more than 4,000 job opportunities. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and is noted as the first Department of Homeland Security office set up in the state. Key Field is named in honor of brothers Fred and Al Key, who set a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, the field supports the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and acts as a facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest non-military employer in the area, providing employment for 2,610 individuals.

Within the city's diverse array of cultural institutions and historic structures are the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Meridian once housed two Carnegie libraries, catering to the white and African American communities. The Carnegie Branch Library, now demolished, was among the many Carnegie libraries established for African Americans in the Southern United States during the segregation period.

The city has been chosen as the future site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. Jimmie Rodgers, commonly known as the "Father of Country Music," was born in Meridian. Within Highland Park, there is a museum that showcases memorabilia honoring his life and career, along with artifacts from the steam engine era. The park also features the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, which is designated as a National Historic Landmark and is the last remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Other notable individuals from the area include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986; James Chaney, an activist who was murdered during the Mississippi civil rights movement in 1964; and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, which is based in Meridian. The federal courthouse hosted the trial from 1966 to 1967 for those charged in the murders of Chaney and two other activists; this trial was significant as it marked the first occasion a white jury found a white official guilty for a murder associated with civil rights.

The region now known as Meridian was first settled by the Choctaw Native Americans and was acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, amidst the era of Indian Removal. Following the ratification of the treaty, European American settlers began to migrate into the area.

After obtaining a federal land grant of approximately 2,000 acres (810 hectares), Richard McLemore, the inaugural settler of Meridian, began providing free land to attract newcomers and promote growth in the area. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer hailing from Alabama, purchased the majority of McLemore's land. The remaining 80 acres (0.32 km²) were acquired by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Recognized as the city's founders, Ragsdale and Ball started the process of dividing their individual parcels into lots for future development.

A significant dispute emerged regarding the name of the settlement. Ball and the city's industrial inhabitants favored "Meridian," considering it synonymous with "junction." In contrast, the agricultural community supported "<unk>" (which translates to "mad river" in a Native American language), named after a nearby creek. Ragsdale suggested the name "Ragsdale City." To promote the name, Ball constructed a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, where a sign changed daily between "Meridian" and "<unk>." Ultimately, the swift expansion of the railroads drew numerous railroad workers, who outnumbered other residents and ensured that "Meridian" became the station's official name. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the onset of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was merely a small village. Its pivotal location at a railroad junction prompted the Confederacy to establish various military installations to bolster their wartime efforts. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman led his troops into the town, obliterating the railroads in every direction, alongside an arsenal and substantial storage facilities; a significant portion of the town's infrastructure was set ablaze. Sherman is said to have remarked afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." Nevertheless, the railroad lines in the city were swiftly repaired, and operations resumed within just 26 working days following the battle. Throughout the Reconstruction era, racial tensions remained high, as exemplified by the 1871 riot that erupted after a fire damaged several businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town experienced significant growth and entered its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. The introduction of railroads enhanced transportation and attracted various industries, leading to a surge in population. As the resident count increased, business activities thrived in the downtown area. Between 1890 and 1930, Meridian emerged as the largest city in Mississippi and a major manufacturing hub in the Southern region. Many of the city's prominent historical structures were constructed during this period and shortly thereafter, including the Grand Opera House, which opened in 1890, the Wechsler School built in 1894, two Carnegie libraries established in 1913, and the <unk> Building, completed in 1929, which became Meridian's tallest skyscraper.

The city experienced continued expansion, driven by a commission government that aimed to establish 90 new industrial sites in 1913, alongside a flourishing automobile sector in the 1920s. Even in the face of the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, the city managed to draw in new businesses. As people sought escape during the difficult times of the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building opened in downtown Meridian, designed to "offer luxury to the average person," along with the Temple Theater, which functioned as a cinema. Additionally, the federal courthouse was constructed in 1933 as part of a WPA initiative.

Following a short economic slump at the close of the Depression, the nation entered World War II, which revitalized the significance of railroads. The railways were crucial in transporting gasoline and scrap metal for military vehicle production, leading to the resurgence of Meridian as the area's rail hub. This economic recovery persisted until the 1950s when automobiles and the Interstate Highway System became increasingly preferred over passenger trains. The downturn in the railroad industry resulted in substantial job losses, prompting a population decline as workers moved to other locations.

In the 1960s, during the American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian hosted an office for the Council of Federated Organizations (CFO) along with various other activist groups. Local figures like James Chaney, alongside Michael <unk>, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman—volunteers from the North—worked to establish a community center that offered classes aimed at empowering African Americans in the region to reclaim their voting rights. This activism incited anger among local white residents, often leading to violence as racial tensions escalated. In June 1964, Chaney, <unk>, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to meet with members of a black church that had been attacked by a bombing and arson. That night, while returning to Meridian, the three went missing. After an extensive FBI investigation, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

At a federal courthouse in Meridian, seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, which included a deputy sheriff, were convicted of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while three others were acquitted during the trial concerning the murders of civil rights advocates in Mississippi. This case marked the first occasion on which a white jury convicted "a white official in a civil rights homicide." In 2005, the state revisited the investigation, leading to charges being filed for the first time. Edgar Ray Killen was found guilty of manslaughter and received a 60-year prison sentence. To commemorate Chaney, a section of 49th Avenue in Meridian was renamed in his honor, and an annual memorial service was established.

Beginning in the 1960s, the growth of highways facilitated commuting, encouraging people to relocate from the city center to newly established housing developments in the northern regions. As strip commercial ventures encroached upon downtown, the city took action in the 1970s and 80s by designating multiple areas as historic districts to maintain the city's architectural integrity. The Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established in 1979, followed by the launch of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street initiated several projects aimed at rejuvenating the downtown area, which featured the establishment of a new Amtrak Station in 1997, designed after the historic train station that once served the city during its Golden Age prior to its demolition. Additional efforts comprised the restoration of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside the encouragement of cohesive urban design. Collaborating with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street played a key role in the renovation and transformation of the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, turning it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of ownership of Meridian Main Street to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, both entities, along with the Meridian Downtown Association, took the lead in revitalizing the downtown area. The Alliance acts as a key organization, providing support staff and resources to the other two groups, and serves as a communication link between them. Although there were intentions to renovate the <unk> Building, newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry postponed those plans in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance is focused on fostering further development and restoration in downtown, aiming to support businesses like specialty shops, restaurants, and bars that contribute to a lively atmosphere both day and night. Concurrently, the Meridian Downtown Association is working to boost foot traffic in the area by coordinating special events, while the Meridian Main Street program seeks to assist the existing businesses in the neighborhood.

Meridian's status as a railway hub has prompted the growth of various hotels catering to travelers. Even prior to Meridian's "Golden Age," several prominent hotels, such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue, were established before the 20th century. The expansion of railroads and the construction of the original Union Station in 1906 led to the establishment of additional hotels for the benefit of passengers and workers alike. The Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian opened its doors in 1907, while the Union Hotel was founded in 1908. In 1979, the Union Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places, and both Hotel Meridian and Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as significant properties within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, its hotels showcased the aspirations of a flourishing economy, particularly exemplified by the Lamar Hotel, an eleven-story high-rise built in 1927. This hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and later repurposed as a county annex building. In 1988, it gained recognition as a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel emerged as a significant venue within the African American business district that arose to the west of the downtown area. During the era of segregation, it was one of the few establishments in the city that offered accommodations for African American travelers.

During the 1960s and 1970s, the expansion of suburban regions led to a significant number of hotels relocating from urban centers. The revitalization of the Riley Center in 2006 heightened the demand for a new hotel in the downtown vicinity. A proposal was made to transform the <unk> Building for this objective; however, the restoration process encountered delays owing to shifts in city administration. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to promote public awareness and backing for the building's restoration, providing first-floor tours and hosting anniversary celebrations.

Meridian boasts nine historic districts recognized on the National Register of Historic Places. The Meridian Downtown Historic District combines two previously established districts: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These locations showcase a variety of architectural styles, predominantly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow styles. Since 1985, Meridian has functioned under a mayor-council or "strong mayor" governance structure. The mayor is elected by the entire voting population every four years. Additionally, five city council members are elected every four years, with each representing one of the five wards, which are regarded as single-member districts. Acting as the city's chief executive officer, the mayor oversees and directs the daily operations of the city government. Meanwhile, the city council operates as the legislative branch, responsible for formulating policies and approving the city's annual budget.

City Hall, which is recognized on the National Register of Historic Places, can be found at 601 23rd Avenue. The current mayor is Percy Bland. The city council is composed of Dr. George M. Thomas representing Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis holds the position of council clerk. Overall, the city employs a total of 570 staff members.

Following Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), making it the sole local DHS in the state. This department manages a jurisdiction that includes nine counties. With $2.5 million in grants secured from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and various organizations, the department initiated training for law enforcement officers from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue methods, in addition to providing civilian courses in basic handgun skills, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearm training. The DHS plays a vital role during emergencies, as seen during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it facilitated the establishment and operation of shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which is comprised of three teams, each serving nine counties.

Since 2009, under the direction of Police Chief Lee <unk>, the Meridian Police Department has comprised 115 full-time officers, in addition to part-time and reserve personnel. That same year, the Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, with 2,000 of those classified as felonies. The crime reports for 2009 indicated a slight increase compared to the year prior. Meridian is acknowledged as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population exceeding 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, located in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Meanwhile, the Meridian Fire Department, under Chief Anthony Clayton's leadership, attended to over 1,600 calls in 2009, which included 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service requests.

In the realm of state politics, the Mississippi Senate district map segments the city into three distinct areas. The northernmost region is part of the 31st State Senate District, represented by Terry Clark Burton (R). A corridor extending from the southwest to the northeast corner of the city falls under the 32nd State Senate District, with Sampson Jackson, II (D) serving as its representative. The western and southeastern parts of the city are included in the 33rd State Senate District, which is held by <unk> Carmichael (R). As for the Mississippi House of Representatives, the city is divided into four districts. The southern and eastern parts are located within House District 81, represented by Steven A. Horne (R). The central area of the city encompasses all of House District 82, which is represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D). Surrounding House District 82 is House District 83, represented by Greg Snowden (R). Finally, the western section of the city, along with a small northern portion, is included in House District 84, represented by Tad Campbell (R).

On the national level, the city falls within Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, which is presently represented by Gregg Harper (R), who has held the position since 2009. Lauderdale County, where Meridian is located, has consistently backed the Republican nominee in every U.S. presidential election since 1972. Before this trend toward the Republican Party, white voters in the area predominantly supported Democratic candidates, as the region was largely under the control of a single party for many years following the late 19th century.

The city's growth has mirrored the influence of various social and economic elements. From its inception until 1970, the population consistently rose with each census, though the rates of growth fluctuated significantly, reaching a high of 165% and dropping to a low of just 0.2%. The census of 1970 noted a decrease in population, but by 1980, there was a marginal increase, followed by a continuous decline until the early 21st century when growth began again. Between 1980 and 2000, the population decreased by over 14%. The census in 2000 recorded a population of 39,968, which corresponded to a density of 885.9 individuals per square mile (342.0/km²). By 2008, the city had become the sixth largest in the state, and a population rise was noted in 2010.

Meridian serves as the central city of the Meridian region, which, as of 2009, included three counties: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, boasting a combined population of 106,139. The population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius is 232,900, and this number rises to 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius.

Although the city's overall population growth has fluctuated, there has been a consistent increase in both the number and proportion of non-white residents. The only reduction in this demographic occurred between 1960 and 1970, coinciding with a significant drop in the city's total population. According to the 2010 Census, the racial composition of the city was 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.09% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Individuals identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race constituted 1.75% of the population.

The 2000 Census recorded a total of 17,890 housing units in the city, with 15,966 of those being occupied; among these, 10,033 were family homes. Of the occupied housing, 31.1% included children under the age of 18, 36.2% were households with married couples, 23.3% were led by a female householder without a spouse, and 37.2% were classified as non-family households. Individuals made up 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% included at least one resident aged 65 or older living alone. The average household size was recorded at 2.39, while families averaged 3.06 members. Since 1970, the average household size has consistently decreased from 3.04. Additionally, the median age in Meridian rose from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The median income for households in the city stood at $25,085, while the median income for families was $31,062. Males earned a median income of $29,404, compared to $19,702 for females. The city’s per capita income was noted to be $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population were living below the poverty line, which included 40.8% of individuals younger than 18 years and 22.0% of those aged 65 and older.

The residents of Meridian and the surrounding areas show significant religious involvement, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County inhabitants reporting membership in a religious organization, surpassing the national average of 50.2%. In the year 2000, among those who identified with a religion, 30,068 people (59.0%) were affiliated with the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) were members of the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were linked to the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe played a significant role in the city's economic growth by establishing a variety of businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, right before the city's "Golden Age." By 1927, Meridian boasted the largest Jewish community in the state, numbering 575 individuals. Currently, fewer than 40 Jews reside in Meridian, the majority of whom are senior citizens.

Meridian is situated in Mississippi's North Central Hills region, specifically within Lauderdale County. According to the United States Census Bureau, the city spans a total area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), which encompasses 45.1 square miles (117 km²) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) of water. In terms of its proximity to major highways, Meridian is located 93 miles (150 km) to the east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) to the west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) to the northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) to the southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) to the west of Atlanta, Georgia. The landscape around the city is characterized by fields of cotton and corn, as well as oak and pine forests, presenting a terrain of clay hills and lowlands near the headwaters of an unnamed river.

The city's urban core has altered its natural landscape through leveling, yet the surrounding regions continue to feature their softly undulating hills. Scattered throughout the city are many small creeks, along with lakes and wooded areas situated in the northern and southern sections. <unk> Creek runs through the southern region and splits into Gallagher's Creek, which traverses the city's center. In the far west lies Loper's Creek, while a variety of smaller creeks, such as Shearer’s Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are spread throughout the city.

Meridian is situated in a humid subtropical climate zone. In the summer season (June through August), the average high temperature hovers around 90 °F (32 °C), accompanied by an average low of roughly 70 °F (21 °C). Conversely, in the winter months (December to February), the average high temperature drops to about 60 °F (16 °C), with the average low plummeting to approximately 35 °F (2 °C). July generally records the highest temperatures, with an average high of 92.9 °F (33.8 °C), while January is noted as the coldest month, featuring an average low of 34.7 °F (1.5 °C).

The city's annual average precipitation is 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Rainfall is relatively consistent throughout the year, with March being the wettest month, receiving an average of 6.93 inches (176 mm). A significant portion of this precipitation is due to thunderstorms, which are prevalent in the summer months but can happen at any time of the year. Severe thunderstorms can bring damaging winds and large hail, in addition to the typical risks associated with lightning and heavy rainfall. These extreme weather events are most frequently seen in the spring, with another peak during the fall. Additionally, these storms have the potential to produce tornadoes.

During its early development, the economy heavily relied on the railroads in the region. By the dawn of the 20th century, the city had become the largest in Mississippi, featuring five primary rail lines and 44 trains running each day. The local economy was closely tied not only to the railroads but also to the goods they carried, including timber and cotton. Between approximately 1890 and 1930, these industries reliant on railroads helped position the city as a significant economic force within the state and its surrounding areas. Although the city encountered economic difficulties due to the decline of the railroad industry in the 1950s, it successfully transitioned from a railroad-dominated economy to a more diversified one, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing now representing the majority of jobs.

Meridian, along with Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, benefits from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established by local entrepreneurs in 1996. By April 2010, the city had a civilian labor force of 15,420, with a population of 232,900 within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, translating to labor force figures of 104,600 and 234,200, respectively. Consequently, the city functions as a center for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Eighty percent of the workforce in Lauderdale County lives within the county, while 90% reside within 45 miles.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's healthcare sector employed a total of 6,260 individuals. The largest healthcare provider in the area is Rush Hospital, which has a staff of 2,610, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500 employees and Anderson Hospital with a workforce of 1,475. Meridian is home to three hospitals and a range of other healthcare establishments. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers services such as cardiovascular surgery, a Level II neonatal intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital, in collaboration with Rush Health Systems, manages the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, which specializes in long-term care for patients who need prolonged recovery in a hospital environment. Riley Hospital features two centers focused on stroke treatment and rehabilitation services. Other healthcare facilities in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has been a community resource since 1882.

Retail is vital for employment in the county, with 5,280 individuals working in this sector as of April 2010. Each year, approximately $2 billion is allocated to retail spending in the city. The Bonita Lakes Mall spans 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²) and features over one hundred shopping options, including department stores, specialty boutiques, dining establishments, and United Artists Theatres. The first phase of the Meridian Crossroads shopping center, which covers 375,000 square feet (34,800 m²) in the Bonita Lakes area, was finished in November 2007, significantly enhancing the local retail landscape. Additionally, the shopping district on North Hills Street has been growing, with new retail and office spaces launching in March 2007 close to the Walmart Supercenter on Highway 19.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively generate over 4,000 employment opportunities for the local population. NAS Meridian is responsible for training naval carrier pilots and various enlisted personnel, and it hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCDTA), which offers drug enforcement training to law enforcement agencies across several southeastern states. The city proudly boasts the first local Department of Homeland Security in the state and plays a pivotal role as the leader of a nine-county regional response team, in addition to a twenty-nine county regional response task force. Key Field holds historical importance due to the record-setting endurance flight by brothers Fred and Al Key in 1935. Currently, Key Field accommodates the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and acts as a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Furthermore, the site features an exhibit dedicated to aviation history and hosts Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County had a workforce of 2,850 individuals in the manufacturing industry. The Peavey Electronics Corporation, which has been producing guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment since 1965, is located in the city. Additional companies in the region comprise Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. The city also features four industrial parks.

Located in the heart of downtown, the MSU Riley Center brings in income through tourism and the promotion of arts and entertainment. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and performances. Meanwhile, Loeb's Department Store on Front St has been a significant clothing retailer in Mississippi, staying in family ownership for four generations. Established by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has reliably offered high-quality apparel for both men and women.

With a vibrant artistic legacy that stretches over a century, Meridian is home to an array of cultural organizations and events. The Meridian Art League, one of the city's earliest art institutions, was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian; however, in 1949, the organization rebranded as the Meridian Art Association and began presenting exhibitions in different venues across the city. Following the closure of the Carnegie Library at 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association transformed the location into the Meridian Museum of Art, offering a dedicated space for its exhibits. The museum first opened its doors in 1970 and has since hosted rotating exhibitions alongside a variety of educational programs aimed at both adults and students. Each year, the museum presents over thirty exhibitions showcasing a diverse range of works, including traditional decorative arts, ethnographic and tribal artifacts, photography, crafts, and more. The collection features portraits from the 18th and 19th centuries, 20th-century photography, and an assortment of sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was established in 1978 as the official arts agency for both Meridian and Lauderdale County. MCA manages the Community Art Grants program, organizes the annual <unk> Festival, offers various workshops, and coordinates numerous special events each year. The council collaborates with a variety of arts organizations in the city and county, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, recognized as one of the oldest subscription community theaters in the South, was constructed in 1932 and attracts over 22,000 patrons each season, making it Mississippi's most frequented community theater. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (<unk>), founded in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and launched its first complete season in 1963. In 1965, the <unk> featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, performing with the orchestra. Additionally, the Orchestra has supported the Meridian Public School District in establishing its own orchestra and strings programs, and played a role in creating the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, who has conducted since 1991, currently leads the orchestra, which is set to commemorate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House, established in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, has a rich history of showcasing various renowned artists and performances, starting with a German company's presentation of Johann Strauss II’s "The Gypsy Baron." However, the opera house ceased operations in the late 1920s as a result of the Great Depression and remained neglected for almost seventy years. In 2000, a major restoration initiative was launched, funded by a $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation, which was formed locally in 1998, along with an extra $15 million from a mix of city, county, and federal resources. The renovation was finalized in September 2006, and the venue was renamed the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live events, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space, drawing more than 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian annually for conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is rightfully celebrated as an architectural gem, recognized as one of the most well-preserved cities from the early 20th century in the United States. Architecture students from various universities across the U.S. and Canada frequently visit Meridian in groups for their studies, attracted by the numerous structures designed by prominent architects. The lyrics describe the surgical experiments conducted by Mengele on inmates at Auschwitz during World War II. His studies targeted specific groups, notably dwarfs and twins, and included both physical and psychological assessments. The song "Angel of Death" references various procedures he performed, including surgeries without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, isolation for testing endurance, gassing, lethal pathogen injections, sex reassignment surgeries, and the removal of organs and limbs, among others.

"Joining forces, but it's only a matter of time before you tear yourselves apart," is a phrase from the penultimate verse that addresses the claim that Mengele performed experiments on twins, one of whom was physically deformed. Reports indicate that "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back, with their wrists also connected." This claim was initially revealed by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, often referred to as the "architect of the Holocaust." It was alleged that Mengele "joined their veins" and transformed them into Siamese twins. This claim received increased attention when Vera Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary The Search for Mengele, which has been referenced by numerous authors, including Gerald Posner, an established expert on Mengele.

The lyrics of "Angel of Death" played a crucial role in postponing the launch of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Although the band had an agreement with Def Jam Records, their distributor, Columbia Records, declined to release the album out of concern for its lyrical themes and cover artwork, which they considered "excessively graphic." Ultimately, Reign in Blood was released by Geffen Records on October 7, 1986. Nonetheless, because of the surrounding controversy, the album was excluded from Geffen Records' official release schedule.
